required_facts.statement: A RACI chart assigns roles by task to clarify who does work and who owns the outcome.
Responsible identifies the person or people doing the work.
Accountable identifies the one person ultimately answerable for a task’s completion.
Consulted identifies people whose input is needed, using two-way communication.
Informed identifies people kept updated, using one-way communication.
List tasks against stakeholders and assign the appropriate R, A, C, or I entries, checking that each task has one accountable owner.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/raci-chart — How to create a RACI chart

text.content: Imagine the task is reviewing delivery-instruction requirements. A hypothetical RACI row assigns the BA as Responsible for doing the review preparation, the operations manager as Accountable for the task’s completion, dispatch and sales as Consulted, and the sponsor as Informed.

text.title: RACI Matrix
text.content: A RACI chart assigns roles by task to clarify who does work and who owns the outcome.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Responsible identifies the person or people doing the work. Accountable identifies the one person ultimately answerable for a task’s completion. Consulted identifies people whose input is needed, using two-way communication. Informed identifies people kept updated, using one-way communication. List tasks against stakeholders and assign the appropriate R, A, C, or I entries, checking that each task has one accountable owner.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Read each letter as a different relationship to this task. Responsible identifies the person or people doing the work. Accountable identifies the one person ultimately answerable for completion. Consulted participants provide input through two-way communication; Informed participants receive updates through one-way communication. The row therefore does not simply mark who attends a meeting.

Build the chart by listing tasks against stakeholders and assigning appropriate R, A, C, or I entries. For a second example task, “Prepare an instruction-access demonstration,” the role assignments might differ. Do not carry the first row’s assignments over merely because the same people are involved. Check that each task has one accountable owner.

In the first row, asking dispatch for input fits C; sending the sponsor a progress update fits I. If two people are marked A for the same task, the row does not meet the one-accountable-owner check. Resolve the ownership assignment rather than leaving two competing A entries. The useful result is task-specific clarity about work, ownership, consultation, and updates, not a general ranking of stakeholder seniority.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Responsible and Accountable are not interchangeable. Several people can do the work, while the task has one ultimately answerable owner. Consulted also differs from Informed: input requires two-way communication; receiving an update is one-way.

practice_anchor.objective: Build a RACI matrix for a hypothetical delivery-instruction mini-project with five tasks: prepare the requirements review, review delivery-instruction requirements, prepare an instruction-access demonstration, gather dispatch and sales input, and provide a sponsor progress update. Use the BA, operations manager, dispatch, sales, and sponsor as stakeholder columns. Given task-specific descriptions of who performs the work, owns completion, provides input, and receives updates, enter the appropriate R, A, C, or I assignments manually.
practice_anchor.success: All five task rows have assignments consistent with the supplied task descriptions. Each row identifies who does the work and exactly one accountable owner; C entries identify two-way input and I entries identify one-way updates. Assignments are task-specific rather than copied automatically between rows. No formulas are needed.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make a five-task RACI matrix visible with tasks as rows, the BA, operations manager, dispatch, sales, and sponsor as columns, and a legend distinguishing R, A, C, and I. Make the single accountable owner in each row easy to check, while distinguishing work assignments from two-way input and one-way updates.

notes: Keep assignments hypothetical; do not prescribe the BA as accountable for business approval.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: A communication plan turns stakeholder analysis into specific ongoing engagement actions.
For each stakeholder group, specify the communication goal, channel, frequency, and owner.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook/plays/stakeholder-communications-plan — 3. Fill out the Communications Plan; 4. Review the Communications Plan

required_facts.statement: Match communication intensity to stakeholder power and interest and review whether the approach is effective.

text.content: Suppose stakeholder analysis shows an operations manager with high power and interest and dispatch staff with high interest but lower power. Engagement planning turns those assessments into specific ongoing communication actions rather than leaving them as labels on a grid.

text.title: Stakeholder Engagement Planning
text.content: A communication plan turns stakeholder analysis into specific ongoing engagement actions.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: For each stakeholder group, specify the communication goal, channel, frequency, and owner. Match communication intensity to stakeholder power and interest and review whether the approach is effective.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
For this hypothetical plan, the manager’s communication goal is to resolve scope decisions. The channel is a short decision meeting, the frequency is weekly during requirements review, and the owner is the BA preparing the materials. Dispatch staff’s goal is to understand current requirements and supply feedback; the channel is a shared update and discussion, with a stated frequency and owner. These channels and timings are examples chosen for this situation, not a mandatory schedule.

For every stakeholder group, make the goal, channel, frequency, and owner explicit. Then check whether the planned intensity fits the group’s power and interest. An assessment has practical value only when it informs actual engagement choices.

Review effectiveness too. If a group remains unclear about what is being agreed, consider whether the approach is meeting its communication goal. The plan is not merely proof that messages were sent. It should connect who is involved, why communication is needed, how it will occur, and who owns it. The example stays within communication planning; it does not transfer business decision authority to the person sending the update.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: A list of channels is not yet an engagement plan. Each group needs a communication goal, frequency, and owner as well. Sending an update also does not by itself establish that the approach is effective; review it against the intended engagement goal.

practice_anchor.objective: Using a supplied stakeholder register for the hypothetical business situation, draft one engagement plan row for each of three stakeholder groups. Specify each group's communication goal, channel, frequency, and owner, using its power and interest to guide the choices. Use plain entries only; no formulas are needed.
practice_anchor.success: All three rows specify a goal, channel, frequency, and owner. Communication choices are justified by the supplied stakeholder needs, power, and interest rather than a universal schedule. For each group, identify what evidence would indicate that the approach is meeting its communication goal.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the connection between stakeholder analysis and engagement actions visible in an annotated table showing stakeholder group, power, interest, communication goal, channel, frequency, and owner. Highlight how the hypothetical operations manager and dispatch staff receive different engagement approaches, with a note to review effectiveness against each goal.

notes: Use example frequencies only, not universal stakeholder rules.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: A workshop facilitator supports the group’s process by planning, guiding, and managing collaborative work.
Use an agenda whose activities and allotted time support the meeting’s goals.
Redirect dominating contributions toward shared goals or invite other participants to balance the discussion.
source_refs: nngroup_articles#https://www.nngroup.com/articles/dominating-workshop-participants/ — How to Navigate Dominating Behaviors in a Workshop

required_facts.statement: Use silent individual contributions when verbal discussion prevents equitable participation.

text.content: Imagine a requirements meeting where one sales representative answers every question before dispatch staff can speak. The facilitator’s task is to support the group’s collaborative process, not to let the loudest contribution become the whole record.

text.title: Meeting and Workshop Facilitation
text.content: A workshop facilitator supports the group’s process by planning, guiding, and managing collaborative work.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Use an agenda whose activities and allotted time support the meeting’s goals. Redirect dominating contributions toward shared goals or invite other participants to balance the discussion. Use silent individual contributions when verbal discussion prevents equitable participation.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Plan an agenda with activities and allotted time that support the meeting’s goal. For this example, the goal is to clarify delivery-instruction needs, so allocate time for individual input, shared discussion, and consolidating the needs. During discussion, redirect a dominating contribution toward the shared goal or invite others to contribute: “We have the sales perspective; what does dispatch need at that point?” This keeps guidance connected to the work rather than making it a contest between participants.

If verbal discussion still prevents equitable participation, use silent individual contributions. Participants could each write the instruction information they need before the group discusses it. That is an example of the supported technique, not a claim that silent writing is required in every meeting.

The facilitator plans, guides, and manages the process so the group can work collaboratively. The useful result is not merely finishing every agenda item on time: activities and time need to support the goals, and discussion needs room for balanced contributions. Keep the facilitation intervention focused on participation and shared purpose rather than deciding whose requirement is correct on the group’s behalf.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Facilitation is not the same as speaking most or choosing the group’s solution. Redirecting dominance and inviting input support the collaborative process. Silent contributions are an option when verbal discussion prevents equitable participation, not a compulsory ritual for every workshop.

practice_anchor.objective: Given a delivery-instruction requirements meeting where a sales representative repeatedly answers before dispatch staff can contribute, choose and justify a facilitation intervention. If invitations do not restore equitable participation, choose an appropriate next intervention.
practice_anchor.success: Select redirection toward the shared delivery-instruction goal or an invitation for dispatch input, explaining how it balances participation. When verbal discussion continues to prevent equitable participation, select silent individual writing before shared discussion and explain how it gives each participant room to contribute.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the delivery-instruction meeting scenario, the participation problem, and the learner's selected facilitation intervention and justification visible.

media.group_title: Guide contributions and make room for individual thinking

segments.label: Manage speaking turns with input signals and a silent start
segments.summary: A facilitator can help keep a complex discussion on time and on track by letting participants signal the kind of contribution they want to make. In this example, yellow cards indicate questions, green cards indicate answers or clarification, blue cards indicate comments or opinions, and red cards indicate observations about the discussion. These signals help the facilitator choose whom to invite next rather than relying only on raised hands. The presenter prioritizes clarification questions; this is an example approach, not a rule for every meeting. A second technique, a silent start, gives participants two or three minutes to think individually and write notes before discussion begins, so they arrive with contributions prepared.

bridge_note.before: Watch how input signals help the facilitator choose speaking turns and how a silent start prepares contributions. The card colors, question-first order, and timing are example choices, not universal requirements.
bridge_note.after: The clip illustrates process guidance and participation techniques. It does not teach goal-aligned agenda planning; the text covers that requirement and explains when to redirect dominance or use silent individual contributions.

notes: Do not introduce consensus or voting as substitutes for balanced participation.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: Different stakeholders may have conflicting goals and different measures of success.
Build shared understanding by involving stakeholders in discussion of goals and evidence rather than presenting an isolated solution.
Forced ranking or dot voting can help a group move toward consensus.
source_refs: nngroup_articles#https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ux-workshop-agendas/ — Step 3: Pick processes that will answer the questions

text.content: Suppose sales wants very few fields on a delivery-instruction form, while dispatch wants enough information to avoid clarification calls. Their goals and measures of success differ: one emphasizes easy entry, the other complete dispatch information. Naming that difference is more useful than presenting one side’s preferred design as an isolated solution.

text.title: Consensus Building and Conflict Resolution
text.content: Different stakeholders may have conflicting goals and different measures of success.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Build shared understanding by involving stakeholders in discussion of goals and evidence rather than presenting an isolated solution. Forced ranking or dot voting can help a group move toward consensus.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Bring stakeholders into discussion of the goals and evidence. For this hypothetical case, examine examples of instruction entry and clarification work together. Ask what each group is trying to achieve and which evidence relates to that goal. The purpose is shared understanding of the competing needs, not hiding the disagreement behind a vague claim that everyone wants a better process.

Forced ranking or dot voting can help the group move toward consensus. For example, participants could rank the information needs being discussed or place dots beside the needs they consider most important. The technique supports movement toward agreement; a ranking does not itself establish that the selected solution is correct.

The useful BA contribution is a discussion in which stakeholders can see one another’s goals and evidence before moving toward a shared position. Keep any remaining disagreement visible rather than announcing consensus merely because a voting activity took place. The example fields and goals are hypothetical prompts for that discussion.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Consensus building is not presenting a ready-made solution and asking for compliance. Voting or ranking can help, but the supported claim is that these techniques can move a group toward consensus—not that a vote guarantees complete agreement or correctness.

practice_anchor.objective: Role-play facilitating a requirement disagreement between sales and dispatch about a delivery-instruction form. Elicit each stakeholder’s goals and relevant examples, then use forced ranking or dot voting on the information needs under discussion.
practice_anchor.success: Both stakeholders’ goals and supporting examples are surfaced before the named technique is applied. The learner uses the ranking or voting results to discuss a possible shared position, records remaining disagreement, and does not treat the result as binding or proof of correctness.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make sales’ goal of easy entry and dispatch’s goal of complete dispatch information visible side by side, together with their supporting examples, the ranked or dot-voted information needs, and any unresolved disagreement.

media.group_title: Surface concerns and revise a proposal

segments.label: Discuss competing stakeholder concerns before revising a proposal
segments.summary: A facilitator proposes another workshop in two weeks and invites participants to express support or disagreement. Participants raise different concerns: timing, accommodating people already present, pressure from a strongly expressed preference, preserving conflict-resolution content, and availability across time zones. The facilitator gathers and summarizes these concerns, then proposes a scheduling poll and an agenda participants can add to, with conflict resolution included. A further response check suggests support for the revised proposal, but does not establish that every concern has been resolved. The exchange illustrates how discussion of participants’ goals and constraints can inform a revised proposal rather than treating initial support as sufficient.

bridge_note.before: Watch how the facilitator invites dissent and gathers competing concerns before revising the proposal. Treat the closing claim of consensus as an initial response check, not proof that everyone agrees.
bridge_note.after: The clip illustrates discussion and revision, but does not teach forced ranking or dot voting. The text explains these techniques and why neither guarantees agreement or correctness.

notes: Avoid unsupported negotiation frameworks or claims that majority vote is binding.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: An event is something that happens during a process and is drawn as a circle.
A task is an atomic activity and is drawn as a rounded rectangle.
A gateway controls branching and convergence of sequence flows and is drawn as a diamond.
Sequence flow is a solid line with a solid arrowhead indicating the order of activities within a process.
Message flow is a dashed line with an open arrowhead and open circle showing messages between separate participants.
Draw activities and appropriate events or gateways, connecting execution order with sequence flows and communication between participants with message flows.

Select a thin single-circle start event to show where a process starts, a thin double-circle intermediate event for something occurring between its start and end, and a thick single-circle end event to show where a process path ends.
source_refs: bpmn_spec#https://www.omg.org/spec/BPMN/2.0.2/PDF — 10.5 — Events; 10.5.2 — Start Event; 10.5.3 — End Event; 10.5.4 — Intermediate Event

text.content: Imagine representing a simple dispatch process: an order arrives, staff prepare it, a decision determines whether clarification is needed, and the path ends after dispatch preparation. BPMN notation gives each kind of element a distinct visual role rather than drawing every step as the same box.

text.title: BPMN 2.0 Core Notation Elements
text.content: An event is something that happens during a process and is drawn as a circle.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: A task is an atomic activity and is drawn as a rounded rectangle. A gateway controls branching and convergence of sequence flows and is drawn as a diamond. Sequence flow is a solid line with a solid arrowhead indicating the order of activities within a process. Message flow is a dashed line with an open arrowhead and open circle showing messages between separate participants. Draw activities and appropriate events or gateways, connecting execution order with sequence flows and communication between participants with message flows. Select a thin single-circle start event to show where a process starts, a thin double-circle intermediate event for something occurring between its start and end, and a thick single-circle end event to show where a process path ends.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Draw the arrival as a thin single-circle start event and “Prepare order” as a rounded-rectangle task. Draw the branching decision as a diamond gateway. Connect execution order within the process using solid lines with solid arrowheads: these are sequence flows. If something occurs between start and end, select a thin double-circle intermediate event; mark the end of a process path with a thick single-circle end event. The example does not require every event type on every path.

Suppose dispatch sends a request to a separate participant, such as an external delivery service. Represent that communication with a dashed message flow having an open circle and open arrowhead, not with the solid sequence flow used for execution order. The diagram now distinguishes something happening, an atomic activity, routing, and communication between participants.

When reading it back, name both the element and what it represents in this process. “Diamond” describes the shape; “gateway controlling branching and convergence” explains its function. Keep the notation tied to the work rather than memorizing disconnected shapes.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: A sequence flow and a message flow do different jobs. Solid sequence arrows indicate execution order within a process; dashed message flows show communication between separate participants. Start, intermediate, and end events are also distinguished by their circle outlines, not all drawn identically.

practice_anchor.objective: Draw a five-step dispatch process using core BPMN notation: order arrival, Prepare order, a clarification decision, dispatch preparation, and the end of the process path. Include a clarification branch that returns to preparation and a message to a separate external delivery service.
practice_anchor.success: The drawing uses a thin single-circle start event for arrival, rounded rectangles for the two atomic activities, a diamond gateway for branching and convergence, and a thick single-circle end event. Solid lines with solid arrowheads connect execution order within the process, including the clarification branch; a dashed line with an open circle and open arrowhead represents communication with the separate external delivery service.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the five-step dispatch process visible with distinct event, task, and gateway shapes, execution-order connections, and separate-participant communication. Include a notation key contrasting thin single-circle start, thin double-circle intermediate, and thick single-circle end events without requiring every event type in the process.

notes: Teach only supported core shapes and flows; avoid gateway subtypes, pools, lanes, and advanced markers.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: An as-is process map records the current process rather than a proposed redesign.
Identify the process’s start and end, collect information about its steps and decisions, and determine their sequence.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/process-mapping — How to create a process map

required_facts.statement: Represent the observed activities and routing with BPMN tasks, events, gateways, and sequence flows.
Review the map with those who perform the process to refine its accuracy.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/process-mapping — How to create a process map

text.content: Suppose dispatch work currently begins when an order arrives and ends when preparation is complete. You want a record of that existing behavior, not a cleaner version of what you hope staff will do.

text.title: As-Is Process Modeling
text.content: An as-is process map records the current process rather than a proposed redesign.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Identify the process’s start and end, collect information about its steps and decisions, and determine their sequence. Represent the observed activities and routing with BPMN tasks, events, gateways, and sequence flows. Review the map with those who perform the process to refine its accuracy.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Identify the start and end, then collect information about the actual steps and decisions. In this hypothetical process, staff read the order, check instructions, decide whether clarification is needed, request clarification if necessary, and prepare dispatch. Determine the sequence and routing from that information. Represent the activities with BPMN tasks, use appropriate events and gateways, and connect execution order with sequence flows.

If clarification is inconvenient, keep it in the as-is map when it is part of the current process. Removing it because it looks inefficient would change the map from a current-state record to a proposal. Review the map with people who perform the process. They may explain that clarification happens before another step, or that the map omitted an activity. Refine the map to reflect their review.

The practical output is a current-process model with a supported sequence and routing. Accuracy is the immediate aim here. A later improvement discussion can use that baseline, but the as-is map should not silently merge observed behavior with desired changes.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: As-is means current, not ideal. A troublesome step still belongs if it is part of current work. Review with the people performing the process refines accuracy; it is not permission to replace current behavior with a proposed redesign.

practice_anchor.objective: Convert the hypothetical current dispatch process into an as-is BPMN diagram: begin when an order arrives, read the order, check instructions, route through requesting clarification when needed, and prepare dispatch before ending when preparation is complete. Review the diagram against supplied feedback from a process performer and correct any mismatch.
practice_anchor.success: The diagram preserves the described current activities, uses start and end events, tasks, a clarification gateway, and sequence flows, and routes both clarification outcomes to dispatch preparation. Any supplied performer correction is reflected without replacing current behavior with desired changes.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the current dispatch process visible as a BPMN diagram, showing its boundaries, ordered activities, clarification decision, conditional routes, and return to dispatch preparation.

media.group_title: Represent process activities and routing with BPMN

segments.label: Build a job-application BPMN model with an interview decision
segments.summary: A hypothetical job-application process is represented in a BPMN editor. A start event connects through tasks for creating and submitting an application, attending an interview, reviewing an offer, and submitting acceptance forms, ending with the offer accepted. Sequence flows connect the activities. A gateway named “Called for interview” is then inserted after application submission. Its yes route continues to the interview, while its no route leads to an application-rejected end event. Labeling the outgoing flows makes the routing explicit.

bridge_note.before: Watch how tasks, events, sequence flows, and a gateway represent the supplied job-application scenario. Focus on the notation and routing rather than the editor-specific controls.
bridge_note.after: The clip demonstrates BPMN representation, not current-process investigation or performer validation. The text covers recording current rather than desired behavior, establishing boundaries and sequence from collected information, and reviewing accuracy with process performers.

notes: Keep improvements as a later comparison, not embedded in the as-is map.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: A future-state process map shows how the process is intended to work after improvement.
Use the current-state map to identify improvements and draw a revised map reflecting the proposed changes.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/process-mapping — Benefits of process mapping; How to create a process map

required_facts.statement: Use BPMN tasks, events, gateways, and sequence flows to represent the revised activities and routing.

text.content: Imagine the current dispatch map includes a separate instruction-sheet lookup and a clarification request. The team proposes a future process in which current instructions are available at the order step. A to-be map shows that intended future behavior, not a claim that the change has already happened.

text.title: To-Be Process Modeling
text.content: A future-state process map shows how the process is intended to work after improvement.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Use the current-state map to identify improvements and draw a revised map reflecting the proposed changes. Use BPMN tasks, events, gateways, and sequence flows to represent the revised activities and routing.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Use the current-state map to identify the proposed improvements. In this hypothetical redesign, replace the separate lookup with “Read current instructions on order,” and revise the routing for clarification according to the proposed behavior. Draw the changed activities using BPMN tasks, appropriate events and gateways, and sequence flows. Keep the revised map understandable as a complete proposed process rather than a few isolated change labels.

Read the old and revised sequences separately. The as-is sequence records the current lookup; the to-be sequence reflects the proposed instruction-access change. Their different meanings matter even when both use the same BPMN shapes.

The useful output is a future-state map that explicitly represents intended activities and routing after improvement. The example is a proposal, not evidence of achieved efficiency. A revised diagram can communicate how the process is meant to work while leaving implementation and actual results to their own work.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: To-be does not mean already operating. Do not describe a proposed route as observed behavior or assume that redrawing a process proves an improvement has been achieved. The model represents the intended future state.

practice_anchor.objective: Redesign the supplied as-is dispatch BPMN diagram to implement two stated changes: replace the separate instruction-sheet lookup with a task labeled “Read current instructions on order,” and route clarification requests only when the instructions are unclear, otherwise continuing to dispatch.
practice_anchor.success: The revised diagram represents the intended future process, includes the replacement instruction-reading task, and uses a gateway with clearly labeled routes for clarification needed and clarification not needed. Both routes connect coherently to the remaining dispatch process through BPMN sequence flows, with appropriate start and end events.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the supplied as-is dispatch BPMN diagram beside the proposed to-be diagram, making the replacement instruction-reading task and revised clarification routing visible while distinguishing current behavior from intended future behavior.

notes: Use the current map as input; avoid claiming measured benefits from a proposal.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: Process mapping can expose bottlenecks, redundant efforts, and unnecessary steps.
Inspect the mapped steps and handoffs for obstacles that impede efficient flow.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/process-mapping — How to create a process map

required_facts.statement: Compare current-state and future-state maps to identify specific differences and potential efficiency gains.
List the specific steps or handoffs where the map shows delay, redundancy, or missing work, and review these findings with process stakeholders.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/process-mapping — Benefits of process mapping; 6. Review and validate

required_facts.statement: Identify a bottleneck as a capacity-limited step that cannot keep pace, causing work to accumulate and limiting the whole workflow’s throughput, and cite the observed capacity, throughput, or accumulating-work evidence in the diagram annotation.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/bottlenecks — What is a bottleneck?; 5 strategies to rectify bottlenecks in your workflows and fix them for good — opening identification guidance

text.content: Suppose the dispatch map shows orders accumulating before an approval step. A delay label alone does not establish the full bottleneck explanation. In this hypothetical case, the step can handle ten orders per hour while fifteen arrive, and the waiting work grows. Annotate the map with that capacity and accumulating-work evidence: the step cannot keep pace and limits the workflow’s throughput.

text.title: Process Gap and Bottleneck Analysis
text.content: Process mapping can expose bottlenecks, redundant efforts, and unnecessary steps.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Inspect the mapped steps and handoffs for obstacles that impede efficient flow. Compare current-state and future-state maps to identify specific differences and potential efficiency gains. List the specific steps or handoffs where the map shows delay, redundancy, or missing work, and review these findings with process stakeholders. Identify a bottleneck as a capacity-limited step that cannot keep pace, causing work to accumulate and limiting the whole workflow’s throughput, and cite the observed capacity, throughput, or accumulating-work evidence in the diagram annotation.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Inspect other mapped steps and handoffs for obstacles, redundancy, or missing work. Perhaps the same instructions are copied at two handoffs. List the specific steps where the map shows those issues and review the findings with process stakeholders. Do not group every issue under “bottleneck” merely because it is inconvenient.

Compare current-state and future-state maps too. If the proposal removes one copying step, identify that concrete difference and discuss its potential efficiency gain. A map comparison identifies a proposed difference; it is not itself a measured result.

The output should connect each finding to a location in the process and supporting evidence. For the approval bottleneck, the key evidence is capacity that cannot keep pace, accumulated work, and the resulting throughput limitation. For redundant copying, the finding is repeated effort. These distinctions make the analysis more informative than marking every slow-looking box red.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Not every delay is a bottleneck. The supported bottleneck definition requires a capacity-limited step that cannot keep pace, causing accumulation and limiting throughput. Also label future-state efficiency gains as potential until supported by actual results.

practice_anchor.objective: Annotate supplied current-state and future-state dispatch diagrams to mark the approval bottleneck and the specific difference where the proposed process removes a repeated copying step.
practice_anchor.success: The current-state approval annotation cites capacity of ten orders per hour against fifteen arriving, explains that waiting work grows and limits workflow throughput, and distinguishes this bottleneck from redundant copying. The comparison annotation identifies the removed copying step and describes reduced repeated effort as a potential efficiency gain, not a measured result.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show current-state and future-state dispatch maps side by side, with approval capacity, arrival rate, and accumulating work visible in the current state. Make the repeated copying handoffs and the proposed removal of one copying step visible, with annotations distinguishing the bottleneck from redundancy.

notes: Keep capacity examples hypothetical; distinguish bottlenecks from redundancy and missing work.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: Lean process improvement aims to eliminate waste and improve value delivered by a process.
Inspect a process for non-value-adding steps and propose a change that removes or reduces the identified waste.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/lean-process-improvement — How to apply Lean process improvement within projects — 1. Determine potential areas for improvement; 2. Identify potential solutions

required_facts.statement: Agree an improvement action with the team, implement it, and review its effects to continue improving the process.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/lean-process-improvement — How to apply Lean process improvement within projects

text.content: Imagine the process map shows dispatch instructions copied twice before preparation. The team investigates that repeated effort as a possible non-value-adding step. Lean improvement aims to eliminate waste and improve the value delivered by the process; the example is about examining a specific source of waste, not removing work simply because it takes time.

text.title: Process Improvement Techniques
text.content: Lean process improvement aims to eliminate waste and improve value delivered by a process.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Inspect a process for non-value-adding steps and propose a change that removes or reduces the identified waste. Agree an improvement action with the team, implement it, and review its effects to continue improving the process.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Inspect the copying steps and propose a change that removes or reduces the identified waste. In this hypothetical situation, the team proposes using the current instruction record instead of making a second copy. Agree the improvement action with the team, implement it, and review its effects.

The review might examine whether the repeated copying was reduced and whether the process now delivers the intended value more effectively. Those are questions for the review, not results you can infer from the proposal alone. If the effects show further issues, continue improving the process rather than treating the first change as the final answer.

The BA’s analysis connects an observed process feature, identified waste, an agreed action, and a review of effects. The technique remains grounded in the work: “remove a box from the map” is less informative than explaining which non-value-adding activity is being reduced and then checking the change.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Improvement is not synonymous with deleting as many steps as possible. Inspect for identified non-value-adding work, agree an action, and review its effects after implementation. A proposed simplification is not yet evidence that value or efficiency improved.

practice_anchor.objective: For the hypothetical dispatch bottleneck caused by copying instructions twice before preparation, propose one change that reduces the identified repeated effort and justify its expected effect.
practice_anchor.success: A written proposal identifies the second copying step as the waste to reduce, describes a specific change such as using the current instruction record, and explains how it could reduce repeated effort while preserving the intended value. It distinguishes expected effects from proven results and describes agreeing the action with the team, implementing it, and reviewing whether repeated copying decreased and intended value was preserved.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the hypothetical dispatch process with two instruction-copying steps beside a proposed process using the current instruction record instead of a second copy. Mark the repeated effort being reduced and distinguish the proposed change from effects that still need review after implementation.

notes: Do not add unsupported Lean waste categories or mandatory improvement cycles.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

text.content: Suppose stakeholders say amended delivery instructions require supervisor approval. That approval governs what the deliverable must allow; it should not remain an informal comment outside the requirements record.

text.title: Business Rules Analysis
text.content: Requirements documentation includes assumptions and constraints that govern the work.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Capture required approvals and operating constraints explicitly when documenting what the deliverable must do.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
In this hypothetical entry, document “An amended instruction requires supervisor approval before dispatch preparation continues.” Record the operating constraint explicitly alongside the required behavior. If the team assumes that a supervisor is available during dispatch hours, capture that assumption too rather than leaving it hidden in the sentence.

The distinction is practical: a requested function might be displaying or amending instructions, while the governing approval or constraint limits how the work may proceed. Make those assumptions, constraints, and approvals visible in the requirement record.

Read the requirement record back to stakeholders with the approval made visible. A description that says only “Users can amend instructions” omits the stated governing condition in this example. The useful output is explicit required approval and operating-constraint information linked to what the deliverable must do. The supervisor rule is invented for the exercise, not a general policy for order services.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: An approval rule should not be left as background prose while the function is documented without it. Capture governing assumptions and constraints explicitly. Do not invent company policies or a complete business-rule classification beyond what the requirements evidence supports.

practice_anchor.objective: Extract three business rules from this hypothetical approval process: staff can amend delivery instructions during dispatch hours only; a supervisor must approve each amendment; dispatch preparation remains paused until that approval is recorded. Write each governing condition explicitly alongside the behavior it limits.
practice_anchor.success: A written requirements record states all three conditions: amendments are limited to dispatch hours, each amendment requires supervisor approval, and dispatch preparation cannot resume until approval is recorded. Each condition is linked to the relevant required behavior, without adding unsupported policies.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show an incomplete requirement, 'Users can amend instructions,' beside an annotated requirement that makes supervisor approval and the restriction on continuing dispatch preparation explicit. Display supervisor availability during dispatch hours separately as an assumption to confirm, not an established policy.

notes: Coverage is narrow: focus on explicit approvals, assumptions, and constraints; do not expand to an unsupported rule taxonomy.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.
